Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Sanjay’s first encounter with the world’s violence began the night his village was overrun by armed men while he was only a boy of ten. A single gunshot had cut through the quiet, the wail of a neighbor’s phone, and the desperate shouts of strangers. He was standing on a muddy path when a flash of white light, a police car’s flashing blue, sliced across the darkness, followed by a thundering ambulance that seemed to echo the night’s gunfire. In the days that followed he could not escape the sounds that now trigger the same raw, primal terror: the shrill wail of a siren, the murmur of people recalling a crash, the sight of someone with a fresh wound. Those triggers, by their very immediacy, have plunged Sanjay into hypervigilance, his mind constantly on the lookout for danger. The very thought of uniforms or weapons, whether police or military, pulls him to a place of avoidance; he refuses to wear the crisp white coat of a chef or the steel gleam of a kitchen knife. He has begun to fawn—saying yes, offering extra help—whenever he feels a threat looming, hoping that overt compliance will protect him. The trauma’s memory is fragmented: he can recall the chaotic images, but he can’t find the words to describe them; the narrative comes out numb, as if he is seeing someone else’s nightmare. Each time he recalls, a wave of grief washes over him, and he is flooded with guilt for not doing more to stop the shooting, for surviving while the others did not, and for believing his life is permanently damaged. That guilt has become a driver of his avoidance. He feels the need to keep his distance from anything that might remind him of the uniform, the open field where the shooting took place, or the ambulance’s emergency lights. In the kitchen, he purposely avoids the open stainless‑steel walkways that connect the prep area to the grill, positioning himself behind a glass partition whenever he can. He has even begun to decline opportunities to work in the main dining hall, choosing instead to cook in the back room, where walls enclose him. He has convinced himself that staying compliant and compliant is the only way to ensure he is not perceived as a threat, a thought that reinforces his hypervigilance, his belief that he must always have an escape route ready, and his dread of any potential trigger. The constant state of alertness has begun to shape his perception of the world. He reports that the more he is on guard, the more readily he notices ambulances, conversations about crashes, or the sight of a colleague’s injured hand. His vigilance, in turn, fuels a pattern of avoidance that makes his memory of the event even more elusive; he can’t fully process the images because he is always looking for the next sign of danger. The hyperactive state of mind has also amplified his sense of threat, forcing him to plan escape routes whenever he feels uneasy, even in the familiarity of his kitchen. His avoidance strategies, in turn, have become a source of new suffering. By staying away from the uniform and the open kitchen space, he has isolated himself from coworkers, who now see him as distant and uncooperative. His attempts to remain compliant have earned him praise from the manager but also the impression that he is not truly invested. This has deepened his feelings of inaction guilt—he believes he is not living up to his own expectations and that he should have stood up when the violence first erupted. The avoidance has also kept his memory of the night in a state of numbness; he can see the images only in fragments, unable to place them into words, which heightens his grief when the memory surfaces. In this cycle, every time he avoids a trigger, he reminds himself of the danger and his own perceived inadequacy, tightening the loop of anxiety, guilt, and withdrawal. Now, 34 years later, Sanjay finds himself in a small kitchen in New York, a place that once felt like a sanctuary but now feels like a minefield. The smell of frying onions is enough to set his heart racing, and the hum of the refrigerator feels like a distant siren. He has been canceling shift changes, avoiding the restaurant’s open dining room, and turning down opportunities for promotion because he fears the same triggers will erupt again. The weight of his guilt, the terror of hypervigilance, and the numbness of his memories have become unbearable. He finally decided to seek help, hoping to reclaim a sense of safety in his own body, to learn that his fear is not a sign of weakness, and that perhaps he can learn to breathe through the siren’s wail without spiraling into a flood of grief. His greatest fear is that the cycle will never break, but he clings to the hope that a professional can guide him out of the echoing corridors of his past.
